An encomium is a formal, elaborate, and enthusiastic piece of praise — spoken or written — for a person, a thing, or an achievement. Think of it not as a quick compliment, but as a full, developed tribute: a speech, an essay, or a passage specifically designed to celebrate and honor something or someone in glowing terms.
What makes it different from an ordinary compliment

If you tell a friend "you did a great job," that is a compliment. But an encomium goes far beyond that. It is sustained (it goes on at length), it is deliberate (carefully crafted, not thrown out casually), and it is elevated in tone (formal, respectful, often eloquent). An encomium doesn't just say someone is great — it argues for their greatness with detail, warmth, and effort.

Imagine a retiring teacher who spent 40 years shaping young minds. At her farewell ceremony, a colleague stands up and delivers a ten-minute speech listing her achievements, describing her character, recalling her impact on students, and honoring her legacy. That speech is an encomium.

An encomium is always positive — there is no such thing as a negative encomium. It is also sincere by nature (unlike flattery, which can be hollow and self-serving). It is aimed at honoring, not merely pleasing. And importantly, it has substance — it gives reasons for the praise rather than just declaring admiration out of nowhere.

It can be delivered as a speech (at a ceremony, award event, or retirement dinner), as written text (a book dedication, a tribute essay, a foreword that praises the author), or even as an entire short work in itself (a poem or essay written solely for the purpose of honoring someone).
Real-life situations where you'd encounter an encomium

• A Nobel Prize acceptance speech where a committee chairman lavishes praise on the winner's life's work.
  • The introduction to a biography where the writer spends several paragraphs honoring the subject before the story begins.
  • A Medal of Honor citation read aloud at a military ceremony.
  • A toast at a wedding that goes well beyond "congratulations" and genuinely celebrates the couple's qualities.
  • A book's preface written by a famous author to honor a lesser-known writer whose work deserves more recognition.

In each of these cases, the praise is not casual, not brief, and not accidental. It is deliberate, warm, and crafted with care. That is the signature of an encomium.
How to use it in sentences

• "The senator's colleagues delivered a moving encomium at his retirement banquet."
  • "The documentary was essentially an encomium to the late architect, celebrating every aspect of his vision."
  • "She was embarrassed by the long encomium her boss gave before handing her the award."
  • "The book's opening pages contain a heartfelt encomium to the author's childhood teacher."

Notice how in each case, "encomium" refers to a full piece of sustained, formal praise — not just a sentence or two.

The plural of encomium has two accepted forms: encomiums (the straightforward English plural) and encomia (the classical plural). Both are correct. In everyday writing, encomiums is more commonly seen.
The tone and register of the word itself

The word "encomium" is formal and literary. You would not use it in casual conversation — saying "that speech was quite an encomium" instantly marks you as someone with a sophisticated vocabulary. It belongs in writing about literature, history, rhetoric, or ceremonies. It is the right word when you want to describe praise that is elevated and deliberate, and when a word like "tribute" or "praise" feels too plain for the weight of what is being described.
One final way to lock it in your memory

Picture a grand hall. Tall ceilings, a polished podium. A distinguished speaker rises, clears their throat, and for several minutes speaks only of one person — their brilliance, their courage, their impact, their legacy. The audience is moved. That moment — that speech — is an encomium. It is praise given its fullest, most dignified form.
